Counting every error fairly: the Box-Cox objective

pdmS7 documentation

Source: vignettes/fair-errors.Rmd
fair-errors.Rmd

A calibration can only be as good as its idea of a good fit. NSE, the usual idea, counts every hour’s squared error alike. That sounds fair and is not: an error of 5 m3/s at the peak of a flood counts 2,500 times as much as an error of 0.1 m3/s on a summer recession, though both may be the same 10% of the flow. A calibration by NSE therefore fits a handful of floods closely and the rest of the record loosely. This article shows the effect, and the cure.

A record with a known answer

Three years of synthetic hourly rain through the standard PDM, with errors on the flow that grow with it: each hour is the true flow times a random factor, a 15% error at any flow. Real gauges and models behave much the same way.

rain <- synthetic_rain("2017-10-01", years = 3, dt = 1, seed = 5)
truth <- modifyList(pdm_presets("standard"), list(area_km2 = 25))
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
forcing <- rain[c("time", "rain", "pet")]
set.seed(8)
flow <- run_pdm(model, forcing[c("rain", "pet")], initial_state(model, 0.5))$output$q_m3s
observed <- flow * exp(rnorm(length(flow), 0, 0.15))
scored <- seq_along(observed) > 24 * 90

Where NSE’s attention goes

Run the true model and ask where its squared errors come from: the share of the total that falls in the wettest 1% of hours, against the share in the driest half.

err <- (flow - observed)[scored]
q <- observed[scored]
top <- q >= stats::quantile(q, 0.99)
low <- q <= stats::median(q)
share <- function(e) c(wettest_1pc = sum(e[top]^2), driest_half = sum(e[low]^2)) / sum(e^2)
round(100 * share(err), 1)
#> wettest_1pc driest_half 
#>        57.0         3.1

Even for the true model, the wettest 1% of hours, about 240 of them, carry more than half of the squared error, and the driest half of the record about 3%. Any calibration that minimises squared errors will listen to those hours above all others.

The Box-Cox transform

The cure is to measure the errors on a scale where they are about the same size at every flow. boxcox_flow() does that:

z=(q+c)λ−1λz = \frac{(q + c)^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}

with a small offset cc so that zero flows stay finite. The power λ\lambda sets how hard the large flows are squeezed: λ=1\lambda = 1 leaves the flow as it is, λ=0\lambda = 0 takes its log, and values between are compromises.

qq <- seq(0, 20, length.out = 200)
plot(qq, boxcox_flow(qq, 1), type = "l", ylim = c(-5, 20), xlab = "Flow (m3/s)",
     ylab = "Transformed flow", lwd = 2)
for (l in c(0.5, 0.2, 0)) lines(qq, boxcox_flow(qq, l), lwd = 2, lty = match(l, c(0.5, 0.2, 0)) + 1)
legend("topleft", c("lambda 1 (raw)", "0.5", "0.2", "0 (log)"), lty = 1:4, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

The same errors on the transformed scale:

for (l in c(1, 0.5, 0)) {
  e <- boxcox_flow(flow[scored], l) - boxcox_flow(observed[scored], l)
  cat(sprintf("lambda %.1f: %s\n", l, paste(names(share(e)), sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * share(e)),
                                            collapse = ", ")))
}
#> lambda 1.0: wettest_1pc 57.0%, driest_half 3.1%
#> lambda 0.5: wettest_1pc 13.4%, driest_half 22.7%
#> lambda 0.0: wettest_1pc 1.1%, driest_half 50.7%

With the log, the wettest 1% of hours carry about 1% of the error and the driest half about half: every hour counts alike, which is what least squares assumes.

Choosing the power

The right power is the one that makes the errors the same size at every flow. Fit a model, cut its flows into fifths, and look at the spread of the transformed errors in each:

spread_by_flow <- function(l) {
  e <- boxcox_flow(flow[scored], l) - boxcox_flow(observed[scored], l)
  fifth <- cut(q, stats::quantile(q, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = 1:5)
  round(tapply(e, fifth, stats::sd), 3)
}
rbind(`lambda 1` = spread_by_flow(1), `lambda 0.5` = spread_by_flow(0.5),
      `lambda 0` = spread_by_flow(0))
#>                1     2     3     4     5
#> lambda 1   0.020 0.034 0.037 0.045 0.269
#> lambda 0.5 0.050 0.070 0.069 0.074 0.166
#> lambda 0   0.132 0.148 0.131 0.124 0.155

The columns run from the lowest fifth of flows to the highest. On the raw scale the spread grows many times over; at 0.5 it still grows; with the log it is flat. These errors were made proportional to the flow, so the log is right for them. Real errors usually sit between: the log is often close, 0.2 to 0.5 when the largest flows are better measured than their size suggests (McInerney et al., 2017). Run the same table on your own calibrated model and pick the power that flattens it. The default of the objective, 0.5, is a safe middle.

Calibrating with it

objective = "boxcox" in calibrate_pdm() scores 1 minus NSE on the transformed flows:

start <- modifyList(truth, list(fc = 0.8))
start$distribution$cmax <- 200
lower <- c(fc = 0.6, distribution.cmax = 100, surface.k1 = 1, distribution.b = 0.1)
upper <- c(fc = 1.4, distribution.cmax = 500, surface.k1 = 30, distribution.b = 2)
fits <- lapply(c(nse = "nse", boxcox = "boxcox"), function(o) {
  calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, warmup = 24 * 90, objective = o,
                start = "soil", control = list(maxit = 60))
})
rbind(truth = c(fc = 1, distribution.cmax = 300, surface.k1 = 2, distribution.b = 0.4),
      t(vapply(fits, function(f) f$parameters, numeric(4))))
#>               fc distribution.cmax surface.k1 distribution.b
#> truth  1.0000000          300.0000   2.000000      0.4000000
#> nse    0.9996364          305.3337   1.999157      0.4183938
#> boxcox 1.0043510          301.6843   1.970166      0.4011965

Both come close on a clean synthetic record; the Box-Cox calibration comes closer on the soil store, whose shape b governs the whole range of flows, not only the peaks. On real records, where a few large floods may carry rating errors of 20% or more, the difference is usually larger. boxcox_lambda sets the power; pdm_objectives() and calibrate_pdm_multi() offer the same score as boxcox_loss, so it can sit on a Pareto front beside event scores.

Flows the gauge measures poorly

Not every flow is measured equally well. A rating is tight where it was gauged and loose where it is extrapolated, above the highest gauging. flow_weights() turns what is known about that into a weight for each hour, for the weights of calibrate_pdm():

rating <- data.frame(q = c(0.2, 2, 8), relative = c(0.05, 0.08, 0.15))
w <- flow_weights(observed, uncertainty = rating, highest_gauged = 10)
round(tapply(w, cut(observed, c(0, 0.2, 2, 8, 10, Inf)), mean), 3)
#>  (0,0.2]  (0.2,2]    (2,8]   (8,10] (10,Inf] 
#>    1.000    0.880    0.294    0.111    0.028

The weights are inverse variances: a flow measured to 15% counts (5/15)^2, about a ninth, as much as one measured to 5%. Above the highest gauging each weight is cut again, by extrapolated (a quarter by default). In CAMELS-GB the rating uncertainty comes with each catchment, at six flow percentiles; for an EA gauge, the hydrometry team’s rating review gives it.

calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, objective = "boxcox", weights = w)

In a calibration project

log_auto_calibration() and the stages of pdm_stages() take objective = "boxcox" like any other, and the log records the power used.

Cautions

  • The power is a choice to check, not a constant: run the spread table on your own record.
  • Zero flows need the offset (log_offset, 0.01 m3/s by default) to be small next to the low flows but not so small that the log of near-zero flows dominates.
  • The Box-Cox objective does not replace event checks. It counts the record fairly; the floods still deserve their own look (Getting the floods right).
